summary: Proposes an extension to RSVP that reduces the guaranteed bandwidth of an existing reservation. It applies to individual reservations, aggregates and RSVP tunnels, and extends RFC 2205. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: You reserved a big table at a restaurant but need fewer seats. This lets you shrink the booking without cancelling and rebooking.

questions: how does rsvp partial preemption work
subtitle: A way for RSVP routers to shrink an existing reservation instead of tearing it down when bandwidth is needed elsewhere.

tldr.problem: When a congested router must free bandwidth for a higher-priority reservation, RSVP preempts the lower-priority one completely, even if only a little bandwidth is needed.
tldr.mechanism: The router sends a ResvErr with the new error subcode 102 (ERR_PARTIAL_PREEMPT) and a flowspec showing the most bandwidth the reservation can keep, and it does not send a ResvTear.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints or the deaggregator can adjust to the lower bandwidth (for example with a different codec) and keep the reservation. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2205.

today: RFC 4495 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2006 that updates RFC 2205. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Full Preemption
sections.content:
This RFC extends the Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP, RFC 2205) so that an existing reservation can be reduced in bandwidth instead of being torn down when some of its bandwidth is needed for other purposes. The bandwidth might be reclaimed because of preemption, for example.

With RSVP aggregation (RFC 3175), two aggregates with different priorities can cross the same router interface. When the interface is at capacity and a higher-priority request arrives, the router must either deny it or preempt a lower-priority reservation. Preempting a whole aggregate means packets are discarded while it is re-established, and every individual flow in it is affected. The RFC wants only the minimum bandwidth taken away.

"Full" here does not mean all bandwidth is used. It means all the bandwidth available for RSVP reservations under the applicable policy is used. Explicit Congestion Notification does not help much for this case, because it does not say by how much to reduce, so an application may need several attempts.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone needs a little room, it is silly to throw out everything you brought. Better to just squeeze things together a bit.

sections.title: Individual and Aggregate Scenarios
sections.content:
In the individual example, two routers carry Flow 1 (priority 300) and Flow 2 (priority 100). Each needs 80 units of bandwidth and the RSVP limit on the interface is 100 units. Each flow has an establishing priority and a defending priority, and a flow with a higher establishing priority can take bandwidth from one with a lower defending priority. Without this extension Flow 1 is preempted. With it, the ResvErr can say that 20 units remain available (100 minus 80), so the reservation can stay up and the endpoints can renegotiate, for instance by switching to a lower-bandwidth codec.

In the aggregate example, aggregate X and aggregate Y each reserve 400 kbps (five 80 kbps flows) across a link with 800 kbps of RSVP capacity. Adding Flow 9 to aggregate X creates 880 kbps of offered load against 800 kbps of capacity. Because X has higher priority, plain RSVP would deny all of aggregate Y. The goal is to signal that only 80 kbps needs to be removed from it.
sections.plainLanguage: If you only need 20 more seats, just ask for 20 seats back. Do not clear the whole room.

sections.title: Requirements for Reduction
sections.content:
The RFC lists four requirements that apply to both individual and aggregate reservations.

  • It MUST be possible to tell one reservation from another, and an aggregate from other flows.
  • It MUST be possible to indicate, in an RSVP error message from the congested router, that a specific reservation is to be reduced.
  • The same message MUST carry the new maximum bandwidth the reservation can use, but no more.
  • Retransmitted reduction indications MUST NOT reduce the bandwidth further. Any further reduction MUST be signaled in a new message.

The last point matters because RSVP messages are unreliable and can be lost. If two copies of a "reduce by some amount" message arrived, the router could cut twice as much as intended.
sections.plainLanguage: Say how much room is left, not how much to give up. That way, if the message is read twice, nobody gives up too much.

sections.title: The Reduction Mechanism
sections.content:
A partly failed reservation produces a ResvErr message, as preemptions do today, with the ERROR_SPEC and PREEMPTION_PRI objects. The existing preemption code is Errcode 2 (Policy Control Failure) with ErrSubCode 5 (ERR_PREEMPT). Partial preemption adds ErrSubCode = 102 (ERR_PARTIAL_PREEMPT).

The flowspec in the error flow descriptor gives the highest average and peak rates that the preempting system can accept in the next RESV message. The deaggregator or endpoint must reduce its reservation to that or less, whether by changing codecs, dropping reservations or some other mechanism. The flowspec SHOULD be lower than the original request.

Normally the router that sends a ResvErr downstream also sends a ResvTear upstream. Under this extension, a ResvTear is only generated when the reservation is to be removed completely. When it is only reduced, the router MUST NOT send it. The RFC also RECOMMENDS making ResvErr messages reliable with the mechanisms of RFC 2961.
sections.plainLanguage: The message says: you can keep this much, no more. And the router does not tell everyone upstream that the whole booking is cancelled.

sections.title: Individual, Aggregate and IPsec Cases
sections.content:
For an individual flow, the router sends the ResvErr with the new subcode. The requesting endpoint can negotiate a lower bandwidth with the other endpoint, for example by choosing another codec, and both then issue PATH and RESV messages with the lowered bandwidth.

For an aggregate, the deaggregator receives the ResvErr and decides which individual flows are affected. It can send a reduction ResvErr to one or more flows, or preempt one or several flows with a new ResvErr per RFC 3181 plus a ResvTear upstream for each. Those individual ResvTear messages do not tear down the aggregate. In every case the deaggregator lowers the bandwidth in the Aggregate Resv. Which flows are chosen is out of scope.

An IPsec flow with a reservation is treated as an individual reservation, and the same reduction and preemption rules MUST apply. Finally, bandwidth SHOULD NOT be reduced across multiple reservations at once in response to the same event, because a router that does not know the combined impact may cause wider ill effects than necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: For one person, they pick a smaller meal. For a big group, the group leader decides who gives up a seat.

sections.title: Compatibility and Security
sections.content:
Routers that do not support the extension behave as plain RSVP does today. The RFC states that a mixed network works "as it does without this extension, and no worse". A congested router that lacks the extension sends both ResvErr and ResvTear per RFC 2205, and a downstream router that lacks it handles the ResvErr in the normal way.

The extension does not lessen RSVP security. Two risks are noted. A poor implementation that sends the ResvTear along with the reduction ResvErr would make upstream routers tear down the entire reservation, which hurts aggregates most. And, as with RSVP generally, rogue flows can prematurely terminate valid reservations unless authentication is used, so RSVP authentication is encouraged.

IANA assigned ErrSubCode 102 (ERR_PARTIAL_PREEMPT) under Errcode 2 (Policy Control Failure).
sections.plainLanguage: Old routers just do what they always did, so nothing breaks. The one thing to avoid is accidentally cancelling the whole booking.
